Body mass increases dramatically thereafter, with adults reaching an ultimate wet weight of approximately 992 grams [Wwi = approximately 992 grams], a size that is consistent among large alcids and supports their diving locomotion. Eggs are incubated for a period of 31 days [ab = 31 days] under the sustained warmth of the brood patch, which maintains an internal nest temperature averaging 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This relatively short incubation phase is typical of the family Alcidae and reflects the trade-off between embryo development speed and the risk of egg predation by avian scavengers. Upon hatching, the downy chick is brooded closely by both parents, who alternate foraging trips to gather small fish such as sandeels and capelin. The nestling phase is extremely brief, lasting only until the chick reaches about one-fifth of adult mass, at which point the young murre, still flightless, leaps from the cliff and is accompanied to sea by the male parent. This striking strategy of early colony departure is an adaptation to avoid the high mortality associated with extended exposure on land, and it marks the abrupt transition from parental dependence to a pelagic juvenile stage.

Reproductive output in the Common murre is constrained by the single-egg clutch typical of the genus Uria. Females produce 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = 1 egg per clutch], a remarkably low fecundity that contrasts sharply with many other seabird lineages. Pairs generally raise only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], although replacement clutches may be laid if the first egg is lost early in incubation. This combination of a single-egg clutch and a single annual breeding attempt yields a maximum reproductive rate that is among the lowest of any seabird of comparable body size. The strategy is sustained by exceptionally high adult survival and a prolonged lifespan, which allows individuals to accumulate reproductive success over many seasons. This deferred first breeding, operating at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], means that many individuals perish before ever contributing offspring to the population, a demographic reality that underscores the selective premium placed on adult survivorship.

Physiologically, the thermoregulatory demands of foraging in cold northern waters are considerable, yet the murre maintains a core body temperature of approximately 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] during active diving bouts. This high metabolic set-point supports the intense muscular activity required for wing-propelled pursuit of fish at depths exceeding 100 meters. The species' breeding schedule is tightly synchronized with the spring phytoplankton bloom, which drives the availability of zooplankton and subsequently the forage fish upon which chicks are fed. First-time breeders often recruit to colonies adjacent to their natal site, leading to metapopulation structure along continental shelf edges. Conservation concerns center on the vulnerability of this species to marine heatwaves and shifts in prey distribution, as the single-egg clutch provides no buffer against years of poor foraging conditions. Future work will focus on the interplay between warming ocean temperatures and the timing of colony departure relative to prey phenology.
